title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Prince Vasili was not a man who carefully planned things out. Even less did he deliberately scheme to hurt anyone for his own benefit. He was simply a man of the world who had learned how to get ahead, and getting ahead had become second nature to him. Plans and strategies that he never quite acknowledged to himself, but that made up the entire interest of his life, were constantly forming in his mind, sparked by the people and situations he encountered. He didn't have just one or two such plans going at once, but dozens—some barely taking shape, some nearing completion, and some already falling apart. He never said to himself, for instance, 'This man has influence, so I need to win his trust and use him to get a special appointment.' Nor did he think, 'Pierre is rich, so I should get him to marry my daughter and lend me forty thousand rubles.' But whenever he met someone powerful, his instincts immediately told him that person could be useful, and without any forethought, Prince Vasili would seize the first opportunity to gain his confidence, flatter him, become close to him, and eventually make his request.

He had Pierre right there in Moscow, so he arranged an appointment for him as Gentleman of the Bedchamber—which at the time carried the status of Councilor of State—and insisted the young man come with him to Petersburg and stay at his house. With what looked like absent-mindedness, yet with unwavering confidence that he was doing the right thing, Prince Vasili did everything to get Pierre to marry his daughter. If he had actually planned it all out, he couldn't have been so natural or shown such relaxed familiarity with people both above and below him in social standing. Something always drew him toward those richer and more powerful than himself, and he had a rare talent for choosing exactly the right moment to use people.

Pierre, who had unexpectedly become Count Bezukhov and a rich man, felt so overwhelmed after his recent loneliness and freedom that he could only be by himself in bed. He had to sign papers, visit government offices whose purpose he didn't understand, consult his head steward, inspect his estate near Moscow, and receive a stream of people who had previously ignored his existence but would now have been offended if he hadn't seen them. All of these people—businessmen, relatives, acquaintances—treated the young heir with the greatest friendliness and flattery. They were all obviously convinced of Pierre's fine qualities. He kept hearing things like: 'With your remarkable kindness,' or 'With your excellent heart,' 'You are such an honorable man, Count,' or 'If only he were as clever as you.' He began to genuinely believe in his own exceptional kindness and extraordinary intelligence, especially since, deep down, he had always felt he really was kind and intelligent. Even people who had been unfriendly before now became warm and affectionate. The stern eldest princess, with her long waist and doll-like plastered-down hair, had come to Pierre's room after the funeral. With lowered eyes and frequent blushes, she told him she was sorry about their past disagreements and now felt she had no right to ask anything—only permission, after the blow she had suffered, to stay a few more weeks in the house she loved so much and where she had sacrificed so much. She couldn't hold back her tears. Moved by this transformation in the stiff princess, Pierre took her hand and begged her forgiveness, without knowing what for. From that day on, the eldest princess completely changed toward Pierre and even began knitting him a striped scarf.
"Do this for me, my dear—after all, she had to put up with a great deal from the deceased," said Prince Vasili, handing Pierre a document to sign for the princess's benefit.

Prince Vasili had decided it was necessary to throw this bone—a thirty-thousand-ruble payment—to the poor princess, so it wouldn't occur to her to talk about his role in the affair of the inlaid portfolio. Pierre signed the document, and after that the princess became even kinder. The younger sisters also grew affectionate toward him, especially the youngest, the pretty one with the mole, who often made him feel flustered with her smiles and her own blushing whenever they met.

It seemed so natural to Pierre that everyone liked him, and it would have seemed so strange if anyone hadn't, that he couldn't help believing in the sincerity of those around him. Besides, he was always busy and felt in a constant state of mild, cheerful excitement. He felt like the center of some important movement—that people were always expecting something of him, that if he didn't deliver he would disappoint many people, but if he just did this and that, everything would be fine. And so he did what was asked of him, but that happy outcome always remained somewhere in the future.

More than anyone, Prince Vasili took charge of Pierre's affairs and of Pierre himself during those early days. From the death of Count Bezukhov, he never let go of the young man. He had the manner of someone burdened with business, weary and suffering, who nevertheless wouldn't abandon this helpless youth—after all, the son of his old friend and the owner of such enormous wealth—to the whims of fate and the schemes of villains. During his few days in Moscow after Count Bezukhov's death, he would summon Pierre or visit him, telling him what needed to be done in a tired, confident tone, as if adding each time: 'You know I'm overwhelmed with work and it's purely out of kindness that I bother with you, and you know perfectly well that what I'm proposing is the only sensible option.'

"Well, my dear fellow, tomorrow we're off at last," said Prince Vasili one day, closing his eyes and touching Pierre's elbow, speaking as if they had agreed on this long ago and it couldn't be changed. "We leave tomorrow and I'm giving you a place in my carriage. I'm very glad. All our important business here is settled, and I should have left ages ago. Here's something I received from the chancellor. I asked him on your behalf, and you've been accepted into the diplomatic corps and made a Gentleman of the Bedchamber. A diplomatic career now lies open before you."

Despite the weary confidence with which these words were delivered, Pierre, who had been thinking about his future for a long time, wanted to say something. But Prince Vasili cut him off in that special deep, cooing tone he used in extreme cases when special persuasion was needed—a tone that made interruption impossible.

"But my dear, I did this for my own sake, to satisfy my conscience, and there's nothing to thank me for. No one has ever complained about being loved too much. Besides, you're free—you could drop the whole thing tomorrow. But you'll see everything for yourself when you get to Petersburg. It's time you got away from these terrible memories." Prince Vasili sighed. "Yes, yes, my boy. And my valet can ride in your carriage. Oh, I nearly forgot," he added. "You know, my dear, your father and I had some financial matters between us, so I've collected what was due from the Ryazan estate and I'll keep it. You won't be needing it. We'll sort out the accounts later."
By 'what was due from the Ryazan estate,' Prince Vasili meant several thousand rubles in rent payments from Pierre's peasants, which the prince had pocketed for himself.

In Petersburg, as in Moscow, Pierre found the same atmosphere of warmth and friendliness. He couldn't refuse the position—or rather the rank, since he did nothing—that Prince Vasili had arranged for him. Social obligations, invitations, and engagements were so numerous that here, even more than in Moscow, he felt a sense of bewilderment, bustle, and constant expectation of something good that was always just ahead but never quite arrived.

Many of his former bachelor friends were no longer in Petersburg. The Guards had gone to the front. Dolokhov had been demoted to the ranks. Anatole was somewhere in the provinces with the army. Prince Andrew was abroad. So Pierre had no chance to spend his evenings the way he used to, or to have intimate, heart-to-heart conversations with an older friend he respected. His entire time was consumed by dinners and balls, mostly spent at Prince Vasili's house in the company of the stout princess, his wife, and their beautiful daughter Hélène.
Like everyone else, Anna Pavlovna Scherer showed Pierre the change in attitude that society had adopted toward him.

Before, in Anna Pavlovna's presence, Pierre had always felt that everything he said was out of place, tactless, and awkward—that remarks which seemed clever in his head sounded stupid the moment he spoke them, while Hippolyte's dumbest comments somehow came out witty and clever. Now everything Pierre said was charming. Even if Anna Pavlovna didn't say so directly, he could tell she wanted to and only held back out of respect for his modesty.
In the early winter of 1805-06, Pierre received one of Anna Pavlovna's usual pink invitations, with a note added: 'You will find the beautiful Hélène here, whom it is always a delight to see.'

When he read that line, Pierre felt for the first time that some connection that others could see had formed between him and Hélène. The thought both alarmed him—as if some obligation were being placed on him that he couldn't fulfill—and pleased him as an intriguing possibility.

Anna Pavlovna's party was like the previous one, except this time the novelty she offered her guests was not Mortemart but a diplomat fresh from Berlin, bringing the latest details about Emperor Alexander's visit to Potsdam and how the two great friends had pledged an unbreakable alliance to uphold justice against the enemy of mankind. Anna Pavlovna greeted Pierre with a touch of sadness, clearly referring to the young man's recent loss of his father (everyone felt obligated to remind Pierre how devastated he must be by the death of a father he had barely known), and her sadness matched the grand melancholy she displayed when mentioning Her Most August Majesty the Empress. Pierre felt flattered. Anna Pavlovna arranged the groups in her drawing room with her usual skill. The larger group, which included Prince Vasili and the generals, had the diplomat's attention. Another group gathered around the tea table. Pierre wanted to join the first, but Anna Pavlovna—in the excited state of a battlefield commander with a thousand brilliant ideas and not enough time to execute them all—spotted Pierre, touched his sleeve with her finger, and said:

"Wait, I have something in mind for you this evening." She glanced at Hélène and smiled. "My dear Hélène, be kind to my poor aunt who adores you. Go keep her company for ten minutes. And so it won't be too boring, here is the dear count, who I'm sure won't refuse to go with you."
The beauty went to the aunt, but Anna Pavlovna held Pierre back, looking as if she had some final essential instructions.

"Isn't she magnificent?" she said to Pierre, pointing to the stately beauty gliding away. "And such poise! For such a young woman, such perfect manners! It comes from the heart. The man who wins her will be lucky indeed. With her, even the most ordinary man would have a brilliant position in society. Don't you agree? I just wanted to hear your opinion." And Anna Pavlovna let Pierre go.
Pierre sincerely agreed about Hélène's perfect manners. Whenever he thought of Hélène, it was only of her beauty and her remarkable ability to appear silently dignified in any social setting.

The old aunt received the two young people in her corner but seemed more interested in hiding her adoration for Hélène and showing her fear of Anna Pavlovna. She looked at her niece as if asking what to do with these visitors. As she left them, Anna Pavlovna touched Pierre's sleeve again: "I hope you won't say it's boring at my house again." She glanced at Hélène.

Hélène smiled with a look that said she couldn't imagine anyone seeing her without being enchanted. The aunt coughed, swallowed, and told Hélène in French how pleased she was to see her, then turned to Pierre with the same greeting and the same look. In the middle of a halting, dull conversation, Hélène turned to Pierre with the beautiful, radiant smile she gave everyone. Pierre was so used to that smile, and it meant so little to him, that he paid no attention. The aunt was talking about a collection of snuffboxes that had belonged to Pierre's father, Count Bezukhov, and showed them her own. Princess Hélène asked to see the portrait of the aunt's husband on the lid.
"That's probably by Vinesse," said Pierre, naming a famous miniaturist, and he leaned over the table to take the snuffbox while trying to hear the conversation at the other table.

He half stood up, meaning to walk around, but the aunt handed him the snuffbox across Hélène's back. Hélène leaned forward to make room and looked back with a smile. She was wearing, as always at evening parties, a dress cut very low at the front and back, in the fashion of the time. Her bust, which had always seemed like marble to Pierre, was so close that his nearsighted eyes couldn't help noticing the living warmth of her neck and shoulders, so near his lips that he would only have had to bend his head slightly to touch them. He felt the warmth of her body, smelled her perfume, and heard the creaking of her corset as she moved. He no longer saw her marble beauty as a complete whole unified with her dress—instead, he saw all the charm of her body barely concealed by her clothing. And once he had seen this, he couldn't unsee it, just as you can't restore an illusion you've seen through.

"So you've never noticed before how beautiful I am?" Hélène seemed to say. "You hadn't realized I'm a woman? Yes, I am a woman who could belong to anyone—to you too," said her glance. And at that moment Pierre felt that Hélène not only could but must be his wife, and that it couldn't be any other way.

He knew this as surely as if he had been standing at the altar with her. How and when it would happen he didn't know; he didn't even know if it would be a good thing (he even felt, for some reason he couldn't explain, that it would be a bad thing), but he knew it would happen.

Pierre dropped his eyes, then raised them again, trying to see her once more as a distant beauty far removed from him—the way he had seen her every day until then. But he could no longer do it. He couldn't, just as a man who has mistaken a tuft of steppe grass for a tree through the mist can never see it as a tree again once he recognizes what it is. She was terribly close. She already had power over him. Between them there was no barrier except the barrier of his own will.
"Well, I'll leave you in your little corner," came Anna Pavlovna's voice. "I can see you're doing just fine there."
And Pierre, anxiously trying to remember if he'd done anything wrong, looked around with a blush. It seemed to him that everyone knew what had happened to him, just as he knew it himself.
A little later, when he joined the larger group, Anna Pavlovna said to him: "I hear you're renovating your Petersburg house?"
This was true. The architect had told him it was necessary, and Pierre, without knowing why, was having his enormous Petersburg mansion redone.

"That's a good thing, but don't move out of Prince Vasili's. It's good to have a friend like the prince," she said, smiling at Prince Vasili. "I know a thing or two about that, don't I? And you're still so young. You need advice. Don't be angry with me for exercising an old woman's privilege."

She paused, as women always do after mentioning their age. "If you marry, that will be a different matter," she continued, her glance linking them both. Pierre didn't look at Hélène and she didn't look at him. But she was just as terrifyingly close. He mumbled something and blushed.

When he got home, he couldn't sleep for a long time, thinking about what had happened. What had happened? Nothing. He had simply realized that the woman he had known since childhood—about whom he would say casually when her beauty was mentioned, 'Yes, she's good-looking'—he had realized that this woman could be his.

"But she's stupid. I've said so myself," he thought. "There's something wrong, something ugly, about the feeling she stirs in me. I've been told that her brother Anatole was in love with her and she with him, that there was a real scandal, and that's why he was sent away. Hippolyte is her brother... Prince Vasili is her father... This is wrong..." he reflected. But even as he thought this—and the thought was still incomplete—he caught himself smiling and realized a completely different train of thought had taken over. While thinking about her flaws, he was simultaneously dreaming about how she would be his wife, how she would love him and become entirely different, and how everything he had thought and heard about her might be false. And once again he saw her, not as Prince Vasili's daughter, but her whole body only veiled by its gray dress. "But no! Why didn't this occur to me before?" And again he told himself it was impossible, that there would be something unnatural, something dishonorable about this marriage. He remembered her past words and looks and the words and looks of those who had seen them together. He recalled Anna Pavlovna's comments about his house, remembered a thousand similar hints from Prince Vasili and others, and was seized with terror that he had somehow already bound himself to do something clearly wrong that he ought not to do. But even as he was convincing himself of this, in another part of his mind her image rose in all its feminine beauty.
